The Glacial eelpout, Lycodes frigidus, exhibits a life history closely tied to the frigid, stable environments of the deep Arctic. Females produce yolky, demersal eggs with a diameter of 7 mm, from which hatchlings emerge at a wet weight of 0.18 grams [Wwb = 0.18 grams]. This substantial initial mass, a product of large egg size, provides a considerable yolk reserve that sustains the endotrophic yolk-sac larva through a prolonged period of development. A consistent thermal regime of -0.7 °C [T = -0.7 °C] governs much of the species' physiology; it is within this frigid environment that the larvae complete yolk absorption and transition to an exotrophic feeding mode. The demanding conditions of the deep sea, characterized by low temperatures and sparse food availability, likely contribute to a conservative growth pattern. Data from trawl surveys suggest that the ultimate total length reaches 57 cm [Li = 57 cm], a size indicative of a relatively large-bodied zoarcid that occupies the upper tiers of the benthic invertebrate community.

Sexual maturation in Lycodes frigidus is attained at a total length of approximately 25 cm [Lp = approximately 25 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight of 70 grams [Wwp = 70 grams] according to local length-weight regressions. Reaching this threshold initiates vitellogenesis and the onset of gonadal recrudescence, marking the transition from a growing juvenile to a reproductively viable organism. This length at puberty represents a considerable portion of the species' ultimate total length of 57 cm [Li = 57 cm], suggesting a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth before the energetic demands of reproduction begin. Tagging and recapture studies have provided insights into growth rates, confirming that reaching 25 cm may require several years of slow, steady growth in the cold, oligotrophic waters these fish inhabit. The maturation process is thus a protracted affair, finely tuned to the limited productive capacity of their deep-sea habitat, which constrains the rate at which individual fish can accumulate the necessary body mass.

Reproductive output in this species is modest and paced by the extreme cold. At the ambient temperature of -0.7 °C [T = -0.7 °C], an individual female produces approximately 500 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 500 eggs per year], derived from a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] with approximately 500 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 500 eggs per spawning event]. This low annual fecundity, compared to many temperate zoarcids, exemplifies a strategy of producing numerous eggs given the species' large body size. The observation that a mature female of 70 grams [Wwp = 70 grams] allocates resources to so many offspring is a classic adaptation to an environment where larval survival hinges on a well-provisioned yolk supply for an extended pelagic larval phase. The combination of a single annual clutch and large clutch size suggests a conservative reproductive strategy that maximizes per-offspring investment while taking advantage of the species' large body size and long lifespan.

The remarkable longevity of Lycodes frigidus is a direct corollary of its slow growth and meager reproductive output in the prevailing thermal conditions. At a stable temperature of -0.7 °C [T = -0.7 °C], the species can achieve a maximum lifespan of 12,775 days [am = 12,775 days], a duration that permits the gradual accumulation of mass to the maximum recorded adult body mass of 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams]. Reaching this ultimate wet weight of 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams] from a birth mass of 0.18 grams [Wwb = 0.18 grams] involves an approximately eight-thousand-fold increase over many decades, a testament to the metabolically thrifty lifestyle dictated by the polar deep-sea environment. This extreme lifespan allows for multiple, if infrequent, spawning events throughout an individual's life, reinforcing an iteroparous life-history model where reproductive risk is spread across many years. Senescence appears to be a gradual process, with the oldest individuals showing signs of progressive physiological deterioration only after many decades.

Comparative studies with other deep-water zoarcids, such as Lycodes esmarkii, highlight the hyper-slow pace of life in Lycodes frigidus. The total length at puberty of 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm] is attained at a somatic size of 70 grams [Wwp = 70 grams], after which growth continues toward the asymptotic dimensions of 57 cm [Li = 57 cm] and 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams]. This relationship between structural length and body mass is characteristic of a species that invests heavily in somatic growth before channeling resources into reproduction. The high annual fecundity of 500 eggs per year [Ri = 500 eggs per year], partitioned as one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] with approximately 500 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 500 eggs per clutch], underscores the trade-off between egg number and egg size that is typical of polar teleosts. All life-history events, from the 0.18 gram [Wwb = 0.18 gram] neonate to the senescent adult, occur at the lowest functional limits of metabolic machinery near -0.7 °C [T = -0.7 °C], rendering Lycodes frigidus a fascinating model for understanding life-history evolution under energetic constraints at the polar extremes.
